tagline: A short follow-up letter to a persecuted church, correcting the claim that the Day of the Lord had already come and calling idle members back to work.
overview:
Second Thessalonians is a brief letter in three chapters, sent in the names of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy to the same church in Thessalonica that received 1 Thessalonians. The church was still suffering persecution, and something had shaken it badly: a message, whether by a prophetic word, a spoken report, or a letter claiming to come from Paul, that the Day of the Lord had already arrived. Some members, perhaps unsettled by that belief, had stopped working and were living off others.

The letter answers in three movements. Chapter 1 encourages the suffering believers with the promise that God is just: when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, he will give relief to his afflicted people and bring judgment on those who oppress them. Chapter 2 corrects the false report. The Day of the Lord will not come until a rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness is revealed, a figure who exalts himself against every god and sets himself up in God's temple, but whom the Lord Jesus will destroy at his coming. For now something or someone is restraining him. Chapter 3 asks for prayer and deals firmly but pastorally with those who refuse to work, reminding the church of Paul's own example and of the rule he had taught them: if anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.

The letter is short, and its central passage (2:1-12) is among the most puzzling in the New Testament. But its main concerns are plain: steadiness under pressure, confidence in God's justice, refusal to be stampeded by end-times claims, and ordinary faithfulness in daily work.
author:
The letter names Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy as senders (1:1), and Paul adds a greeting in his own hand as the mark in every letter (3:17). The early church accepted it as Paul's, and it appears in the earliest lists and collections of his letters.

Its authorship is more debated than that of 1 Thessalonians. Scholars who think a later follower of Paul wrote it point to several features: its structure and wording follow 1 Thessalonians very closely, sometimes phrase for phrase, while its tone is cooler and more formal; its teaching about the end seems to differ, since 1 Thessalonians says the Day will come suddenly like a thief, while 2 Thessalonians lists events that must happen first; and the stress on Paul's signature and the warning against a letter seeming to be from us (2:2) could suggest a later writer claiming Paul's authority against other writings in his name. Scholars who hold that Paul wrote it answer that close similarity is exactly what one would expect in two letters written to the same church within weeks or months; that the change of tone suits a letter correcting a misunderstanding; that Jewish and early Christian teaching, including Jesus' own teaching in Mark 13, holds together both the suddenness of the end and signs that precede it; and that Paul had good reason to guard against forged letters if one had in fact reached the church. A few scholars even argue that 2 Thessalonians was written before 1 Thessalonians. The majority of evangelical and many other scholars accept Paul's authorship; a large part of critical scholarship does not.
date: If Paul wrote it, he wrote it from Corinth soon after 1 Thessalonians, around AD 50 or 51, while Silvanus and Timothy were still with him (Acts 18:5); the two letters would then be only weeks or months apart. Scholars who see it as the work of a later writer usually date it toward the end of the first century, often somewhere between AD 70 and 100. Some have connected the reference to the temple of God (2:4) with the period before the temple's destruction in AD 70, which would favor an earlier date, though others read the temple figuratively.
setting: The setting is the same as for 1 Thessalonians: Thessalonica, the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and a free city on the Via Egnatia, where Paul founded a mostly Gentile church around AD 49 or 50 (Acts 17:1-10). The believers had faced hostility from the start, and the persecution had continued and perhaps grown (1:4). Some in the church had been told that the Day of the Lord had already come (2:2); what they meant by that is unclear, but it seems to have unsettled them deeply. Some members had also stopped working and were living disorderly lives, depending on others and meddling in their affairs (3:6-12). In a city where many poor people relied on wealthy patrons, and where the church shared meals and resources, this placed a real burden on others and damaged the church's standing.
purpose: The letter aims to encourage the church to persevere under persecution by assuring them of God's just judgment and of their future relief (chapter 1); to correct the false teaching that the Day of the Lord had already come, by reminding them of what Paul had taught about the events that must come first (2:1-12); to strengthen their confidence that God chose and called them (2:13-17); and to direct the church to deal with members who refused to work, withdrawing from them without treating them as enemies (3:6-15).
story: Second Thessalonians continues the conversation begun in 1 Thessalonians and shows a young church working out what it means to wait for the Lord's coming while living an ordinary life. It draws on the prophets' language for the Day of the Lord and on Daniel's visions of a ruler who exalts himself against God and defiles the sanctuary (Daniel 7 to 11), and it anticipates the later New Testament teaching about antichrists (1 John 2:18) and the beast of Revelation 13. Its place in the story is at the church's beginning, but its subject is the story's end.
christ: The Lord Jesus stands at the center of the letter's hope. He will be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, to be glorified in his saints and to judge those who do not know God (1:7-10). He will destroy the lawless one with the breath of his mouth and the majesty of his arrival (2:8), which echoes the messianic king of Isaiah 11:4. As in 1 Thessalonians, he is named with God the Father as the source of grace and peace (1:2) and of comfort and hope (2:16-17), and the letter even places his name first. The glory of Christ is what believers are called to share (2:14).
reading:
Read 2 Thessalonians as a pastoral correction, not an end-times timetable. Its purpose in chapter 2 is to calm a frightened church, not to satisfy curiosity, and Paul assumes the readers already know what he taught them in person (2:5-6), which means we are overhearing half a conversation. Be honest about what cannot be known: the identity of the restrainer, in particular, has puzzled readers since the early centuries, and Augustine admitted he did not know what Paul meant. Watch for the contrast between the lawless one and the Lord Jesus, and between those who refuse the love of the truth and those whom God chose. Don't miss chapter 3, which brings the whole letter down to earth.

The man of lawlessness has been read in several main ways. Many readers, from Irenaeus in the second century to most modern futurist interpreters, take him as a single person who will appear shortly before Christ's return, the figure later called the Antichrist. Others read the passage against Paul's own century, recalling the emperor Caligula's attempt in AD 40 to have his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple, or pointing to Nero or to the events leading to AD 70. Many Protestant Reformers and some later confessions identified the man of sin with the papacy, a reading few hold today. Still others see a recurring power of rebellion against God that takes shape in many rulers and systems through history and will come to a head at the end. Each reading has its strengths, and the chapter note on 2 Thessalonians 2 sets them out more fully.

structure.title: Encouragement in persecution
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for the church's growing faith and love under persecution and assures them that God will judge their oppressors and give them relief at the revelation of the Lord Jesus.

structure.title: The Day of the Lord has not come
structure.summary: The rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first; the lawless one is now restrained, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him at his coming.

structure.title: Chosen and called
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians for salvation, urges them to stand firm in the traditions they were taught, and prays for their comfort.

structure.title: Request for prayer
structure.summary: Paul asks for prayer for the spread of the word and for deliverance from wicked people, and expresses confidence in the Lord's faithfulness.

structure.title: Warning against idleness and farewell
structure.summary: The church must withdraw from those who refuse to work, following Paul's example, but treat them as brothers, and receive Paul's signed greeting.

themes.title: God's just judgment
themes.body: The letter insists that God is just and that the suffering of his people is not the end of the story. At the revelation of the Lord Jesus, the persecuted will receive relief and those who oppress them and refuse the gospel will receive judgment (1:5-10). This is offered to encourage the persecuted, not to invite them to take vengeance themselves.

themes.title: The Day of the Lord
themes.body: Against the claim that the Day had already come, Paul teaches that it will be preceded by a rebellion and the revelation of the man of lawlessness. The church is not to be shaken by excited reports but to hold to what it was taught. The letter's teaching about the end is meant to steady, not to alarm.

themes.title: Evil restrained and defeated
themes.body: The mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but it is held back, and when it is finally revealed it will be destroyed by the Lord Jesus at his coming (2:6-8). Evil in this letter is real, deceptive, and powerful, but it is never out of God's control.

themes.title: Chosen for salvation
themes.body: Paul sets God's choice of the Thessalonians for salvation, through the Spirit's sanctifying work and belief in the truth, against the deception of those who are perishing (2:13-14). Election here is offered as reason for thanksgiving and stability.

themes.title: Work and order
themes.body: Waiting for the Lord does not excuse anyone from ordinary work. Paul points to his own labor night and day, reminds the church of his rule that those unwilling to work should not eat, and directs them to deal with the idle firmly but as brothers, not enemies (3:6-15).

keyChapters.why: The promise of relief for the persecuted and judgment on their oppressors at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven.
The central and much-debated passage on the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, and the restrainer, followed by thanksgiving for God's choice of the church.
Paul's request for prayer and his instructions about members who refuse to work, with the reminder of his own example.

parts.body:
2 Thessalonians is a short letter, three chapters long, sent in the names of Paul, Silvanus and Timothy to the same young church in Thessalonica that received 1 Thessalonians. It can be read aloud in about eight minutes.

Three things had gone wrong. The church was still being made to suffer by its neighbours. Someone had frightened the believers with a claim that ‘the Day of the Lord has already come’ (2:2). And some members had stopped working and were living off others.

The letter answers each in turn. To the suffering church, it says that God is just, and that when the Lord Jesus comes he will set things right (chapter 1). To the frightened church, it says that the Day has not come, because certain things must happen first, and that the Lord Jesus will defeat every evil when he comes (chapter 2). And to those who would not work, it says: go back to work, quietly, and earn your own bread, while the rest of the church keeps on doing good without growing tired (chapter 3).

The middle of the letter, about ‘the man of lawlessness’, is one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, and Christians have read it in several ways. But the purpose of the whole letter is plain. It was written to steady frightened people: “Now may the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way” (3:16).

The letter names its writers, “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy” (1:1), and Paul signs the end in his own hand: “This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter” (3:17). The early church received it as Paul's, and it is in the earliest lists and collections of his letters.

In modern times many scholars have argued that a follower of Paul wrote it later, in Paul's name. Here are their reasons, as they would put them. Its order and wording follow 1 Thessalonians very closely, sometimes phrase by phrase, while its tone is cooler. Its teaching about the end seems different: the first letter says the Day will come suddenly, like a thief, while this one lists things that must happen first. And its stress on Paul's signature, and its warning about a letter ‘seeming to be from us’ (2:2), could suggest a later writer claiming Paul's authority against other writings.

Many other scholars hold that Paul wrote it. Here are their reasons, as they would put them. Two letters written to the same church within weeks or months would be expected to sound alike. A letter correcting a mistake would be expected to sound firmer. Jewish and early Christian teaching, including Jesus' own words in Mark 13, holds together both the suddenness of the end and signs that come before it. And if a false letter really had reached the church, Paul had every reason to point to his signature.

These notes do not choose. Both views are held by careful scholars. The church has received 2 Thessalonians as Scripture from the beginning. These notes speak of the writer as Paul, as the letter does.

parts.h: When it was written, and what had gone wrong
parts.body:
If Paul wrote it, he wrote it from Corinth not long after the first letter, around AD 50 or 51, while Silvanus and Timothy were still with him (Acts 18:5). The two letters would then be only weeks or months apart. Scholars who think a later follower wrote it usually date it toward the end of the first century, often between AD 70 and 100.

The situation in Thessalonica is clear enough from the letter itself. The persecution had gone on, and perhaps grown (1:4). Then something had shaken the church badly: a message that the Day of the Lord had already come. Paul does not know where it came from. He lists three possibilities: ‘any spirit or message or letter seeming to be from us’ (2:2). A spirit means a word someone claimed came from God; a message, a spoken report; a letter, perhaps one falsely using Paul's name. What people meant by ‘the Day has come’ is not clear either. Perhaps they took their suffering as proof that the end had begun.

And some in the church had stopped working (3:6-12). Paul had already spoken to this in his first letter (1 Thessalonians 4:11-12; 5:14). Why they stopped is not certain. Some think excitement about the end made ordinary work seem pointless. Others note that in Greek and Roman cities many poorer men attached themselves to a rich patron for support, and suggest that some treated the church's generous members that way. The two may have worked together.

Greeting (1:1-2). The same three names as the first letter.

Thanks and justice (1:3-12). Paul thanks God that the church's faith and love keep growing under persecution. God is just: when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, he will give relief to his suffering people and judgment to those who afflict them. Paul prays that God will make them worthy of their calling.

The Day has not come (2:1-12). Do not be shaken. The rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first. Something now holds him back. When he is revealed, the Lord Jesus will destroy him at his coming.

Chosen and steady (2:13-17). In contrast, God chose the Thessalonians to be saved. Stand firm, hold on to what you were taught, and may God comfort your hearts.

Pray, and work (3:1-15). Pray for us; the Lord is faithful. Keep away from those who refuse to work and live off others, as Paul himself did not. But do not treat them as enemies. Warn them as brothers.

Peace and goodbye (3:16-18). A prayer for peace, and Paul's own signature.

Notice how the letter ends. After the great drama of chapter 2, the last word is about earning your bread, doing good without growing tired, and keeping a wayward brother within reach of the family.

The Thessalonians were suffering for their faith. Chapter 1 answers the question every persecuted believer asks: will God do anything about this?

Paul's answer is yes. “After all, it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are oppressed and to us as well” (1:6-7). This will happen “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels” (1:7). Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel “will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might” (1:9).

Three things should be said about these hard words. First, they are written to comfort victims of injustice, not to stir them to hatred. The believers are not told to strike back. Vengeance belongs to God alone, as the law says and as Paul says elsewhere (Romans 12:19). A God who never judged would leave the persecuted without justice.

Second, what the church confesses. Every Christian tradition confesses that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, that his judgment is just, and that to be cut off from the Lord's presence is the greatest loss there is.

Third, where Christians differ. Most of the church through history has read ‘eternal destruction’ as eternal, conscious separation from God's presence and glory. Others, holding a view called conditional immortality, read ‘destruction’ as a final end of existence, eternal in its effect. Both take judgment seriously; they differ on its nature. These notes do not choose. The chapter note on 2 Thessalonians 1 says more, and the Honest Answer ‘Is hell forever, or does it end?’ goes further.

And notice where the passage ends: on the day Christ comes “to be glorified in His saints and regarded with wonder by all who have believed” (1:10). The last word is wonder.

parts.h: The man of lawlessness, and what restrains him (2:1-12)
parts.body:
This is the hardest passage in the letter, and one of the hardest in the New Testament. It is best to begin with what is plain.

The church had been told that the Day of the Lord had already come, and they were frightened. Paul says it has not, and he gives a reason. “Let no one deceive you in any way, for it will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed” (2:3). This figure sets himself above every god and even “will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2:4). For now something, and someone, holds him back (2:6-7). When he is revealed, with false signs and deceptions, “the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of His mouth and annihilate by the majesty of His arrival” (2:8).

Notice what Paul says next: “Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you?” (2:5). And, “you know what is now restraining him” (2:6). The Thessalonians knew what Paul meant. We do not. We are hearing one side of a conversation. Augustine, one of the greatest teachers of the early church, admitted that he did not know what Paul meant.

Christians have read the passage in several main ways. Many, from Irenaeus in the second century to many readers today, take the man of lawlessness to be a single person who will appear just before Christ returns, the figure later called the Antichrist. Others read the passage against Paul's own century: only about ten years before, in AD 40, the emperor Caligula had ordered his statue set up in the temple in Jerusalem, and some point to him, to Nero, or to the war that ended with the temple's destruction in AD 70. Many of the Protestant Reformers read it as speaking of the papacy of their day, a reading written into some confessions of that time; few hold it now, and Catholic Christians have rejected it. Others see a power of rebellion against God that takes shape again and again in rulers and systems, and will come to a head at the end.

On ‘what restrains’ him, suggestions include the Roman Empire and its rule of law, a view found as early as Tertullian; the Holy Spirit, or the Spirit at work through the church; the preaching of the gospel; the archangel Michael; or God himself.

No reading is certain. Each can point to something in the text, and none has settled the question. These notes do not choose, and they identify the man of lawlessness, and the one who restrains him, with no living person, church, nation, leader or movement. People who have done so in every century have been wrong, and they have often done harm.

What Paul meant the passage to do is not in doubt. It was written to steady frightened people, not to feed speculation. The Day has not come. Evil is real, but it is held in check. And it will end with one breath from the Lord Jesus.

Paul reminds the church of a rule he gave them in person: “If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat” (3:10). Some in the church were “leading undisciplined lives and accomplishing nothing but being busybodies” (3:11). Paul tells them “to begin working quietly to earn their own living” (3:12), and tells the rest of the church to keep away from such a person, but “do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (3:15).

This verse is often quoted, and it must be read carefully. Paul is speaking about people in that church who were able to work and refused, and who lived off the generosity of others while meddling in their affairs. The word is ‘unwilling’, not ‘unable’. In the same letters Paul tells the church to ‘help the weak’ (1 Thessalonians 5:14), and the early church took special care of widows, orphans and the sick.

So this verse is never a word against the poor, the sick, the disabled, people who cannot find work, or people who receive help. Using it that way goes against the letter it comes from, and against the whole Bible's care for the poor. God told Israel, “open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11).

Christians differ on how far the verse should reach beyond the church, and on how a society should care for the poor: some put the weight on charity, churches and neighbours, and others also on just laws and public provision. The site's wisdom topic on justice and the poor sets out both. On every view, believers are called to give and to act, and the verse is not a slogan for any side.

Paul's own example is the key. He worked night and day so as not to be a burden (3:8), though he had a right to support (3:9). And he ends with a word for those who do the giving: “But as for you, brothers, do not grow weary in well-doing” (3:13).

God is just. The suffering of God's people is not the end of the story. God sees, and he will set things right when the Lord Jesus is revealed. That is a comfort to the wronged, and it is a reason not to take revenge.

Do not be shaken. The letter's teaching about the end is meant to steady, not to alarm. ‘Not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed’ (2:2) is the first thing Paul asks. Excited claims about the end are to be tested against what the church was taught.

Evil is real, but it is held back. ‘The mystery of lawlessness is already at work’ (2:7). But it is restrained, it will be revealed at the proper time, and it will be destroyed by the Lord Jesus. Nothing in the story is out of God's hands.

Chosen and called. Against those who believe the lie, Paul sets the church: “God has chosen you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth” (2:13). God's choice is a reason for thanks and for standing firm.

Work and order. Waiting for the Lord does not excuse anyone from ordinary work. Hope about the end is meant to make believers faithful in the middle, earning their bread, doing good, and keeping one another close.

Jesus is Lord. In this letter Jesus is named with the Father as the giver of grace, peace, comfort and hope (1:2; 2:16), and the Old Testament's words about the coming of the LORD are spoken of him.

Like the first letter, this one does not quote the Old Testament word for word, but its pictures come from there.

The Lord's coming ‘in blazing fire’ (1:8) recalls Isaiah: “For behold, the LORD will come with fire” (Isaiah 66:15). Those ‘separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might’ (1:9) echo Isaiah's picture of people hiding “from the terror of the LORD and the splendor of His majesty” (Isaiah 2:10). In Isaiah these words describe the LORD himself. Paul speaks them of the Lord Jesus.

Vengeance belonging to God is from the song of Moses: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35).

The man of lawlessness looks like the proud rulers of the prophets. Daniel saw a king who “will exalt and magnify himself above every god” (Daniel 11:36), and whose forces would “set up the abomination of desolation” in the temple (Daniel 11:31). That prophecy is usually linked with the Greek king Antiochus IV, who in 167 BC set up a pagan altar in the temple in Jerusalem. Ezekiel mocked the ruler of Tyre, who said, “I am a god” (Ezekiel 28:2).

And the end of the lawless one is told in words from Isaiah's promised king, who will “slay the wicked with the breath of His lips” (Isaiah 11:4). Paul says the Lord Jesus will do it ‘with the breath of His mouth’ (2:8).

God handing people over to the lie they prefer (2:11) has a sad history in the Old Testament too: “So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices” (Psalm 81:12).

And chapter 3's call to work echoes the law's “Six days you shall labor and do all your work” (Exodus 20:9), while its care for the giver echoes the law's care for the poor.

Read it right after 1 Thessalonians. It continues the same conversation with the same church, and it makes most sense that way.

Read it as a pastor calming a frightened church, not as a timetable of the end. Paul's purpose in chapter 2 is to say ‘not yet’, and ‘do not be shaken’.

Be honest about what cannot be known. Paul says the Thessalonians knew what he meant by ‘what is now restraining him’. We do not, and that is all right. Hold the readings loosely, and hold on tightly to what is plain: the Lord Jesus is coming, and he will defeat every evil.

Do not skip chapter 3. It brings the whole letter down to earth. Hope about the end is meant to make Tuesday faithful.

And let the letter ask you its questions. When you are wronged, do you leave justice to God? What claims about the end have frightened you, and what does Paul say to that fear? Are you doing your part, and are you still doing good without growing weary? And whom have you treated as an enemy who is really a brother?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘Eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord.’ What all Christians confess about judgment, and where they differ.
‘The Day of the Lord has already come.’ What frightened the church, and why Paul said not yet.
‘The man of lawlessness.’ The main readings through history, why none is certain, and why no living person should be named.
‘What is now restraining him.’ The Thessalonians knew; the main suggestions since.
‘God will send them a powerful delusion.’ God giving people over to the lie they chose.
‘Keep away from any brother.’ Discipline that still treats a person as family.
‘If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.’ Said of those who refused, never a word against the poor or those who cannot work.

words.line: The prophets' name for the day God acts to judge and to save. Some told the church it had already come (2:2).
Greek apokalupsis, unveiling. Jesus is Lord now, though hidden; his coming will unveil it (1:7).
Greek olethros, ruin. Christians differ on whether it means unending loss or a final end, eternal in its effect (1:9).
Greek apostasia, revolt or falling away. A great rebellion against God before the Day (2:3).
A figure who sets himself above every god (2:3-4). Who he is has been read in several ways; none is certain.
Greek katechō, to hold back. Paul speaks of ‘what’ restrains and then ‘the one who’ restrains (2:6-7).
Used of Christ's coming (2:1) and, as a dark copy, of the lawless one's (2:9). The counterfeit is no match.
Greek paradosis, what is handed on. Here the apostles' own teaching, by speech or by letter (2:15; 3:6).
Greek ataktōs, out of order, like a soldier out of rank. Living outside the way the church had been taught (3:6, 11).
Not merit earned, but a life that fits the calling God gives, by his grace (1:5, 11-12).
